title: Counting the quiet city
bodyMd:
Original social-science exposition.

A city noise survey once relied on recordings taken beside major roads during the afternoon. Those measurements were useful for estimating traffic exposure, but residents who complained about late-night noise often saw little connection between the published map and their own experience. A residential lane could appear quiet on the map while remaining noisy after midnight.

A pilot survey addressed this mismatch by asking trained residents to follow fixed walking routes at four specified times. Each carried the same type of sound meter and paused at marked locations for sixty seconds. The routes included courtyards and pedestrian lanes as well as main roads. Participants also noted the apparent source of each loud event, though those descriptions were stored separately from the numerical measurements.

The new results did not overturn the earlier traffic findings. Major roads remained loud during the day. They did, however, reveal that some narrow lanes had short, intense peaks at night when deliveries arrived or doors closed outside music venues. These peaks disappeared into averages calculated over an entire day.

The researchers cautioned that volunteers were not a random sample of residents and that a single week could not capture seasonal patterns. Yet the pilot exposed a problem of measurement design: a map can be accurate about what it measures while omitting conditions essential to the people who use it. The next survey will retain roadside monitors and add repeated neighborhood routes in different seasons.
